# Summary {.unnumbered}

We provide estimates of the crop pollination ecosystem service for the 27 Member States of the European Union in 2000, 2006,
2012, 2018 and 2024, following the accounting method of @vallecillo2018[, with the dependency ratios of @siopa2024 and the
bumblebee model projected to each year]{.content-visible unless-meta="method-original"}[, in its original form]{.content-visible when-meta="method-original"}. In 2024, crops that depend on insect pollination
cover {{< fact demand_mha_2024 >}} million hectares, and {{< fact met_pct_2024 >}} percent of that area lies where the
environment can support wild pollinators. The production attributable to the service is {{< fact flow_mt_2024 >}} million
tonnes, against {{< fact flow_mt_2000 >}} million tonnes in 2000, and another {{< fact unmet_mt_2024 >}} million tonnes depend
on pollination but grow outside that area. At constant 2010 prices, the actual flow is worth {{< fact value_flow_bn_2024 >}}
billion euro and the unmet demand {{< fact value_unmet_bn_2024 >}} billion euro. Spatial crop data end in 2018, so the crop
pattern of 2018 stands in for 2024.

# Introduction

Many crops produce more when insects carry pollen between their flowers [@klein2007]. Crop pollination, seen as an ecosystem
service, is this fertilisation of crops by wild insects, which maintains or increases crop production. Ecosystem accounting
treats it as a service that ecosystems supply and farmers use. The direct way to measure it would be to count the insects that
pollinate the flowers of each crop, which cannot be done across a continent, so the accounts rely on models [@vallecillo2018].
They need a measure of what the environment can supply, a measure of where crops need it, and an estimate of what results when
the two overlap. This report describes how we estimated those three quantities and valued the result, why we took each decision
along the way and what the estimates show.

::: {.callout-important}
## How to read the results for 2024
Spatial crop data end in 2018, so a decision was made to use the crop area and yield of 2018 to represent 2024. Data sources
with different methods and crop categories are not mixed within the series. Changes between 2018 and 2024 in demand, flow and
unmet demand therefore reflect pollination potential and national statistics, and they do not reflect any relocation of crops.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Sources of orientation
Two earlier implementations of this service provided orientation. The k.LAB project for this service [@klab2026] informed the
list of inputs, the table of land cover scores, the correspondence between major road categories and OpenStreetMap classes,
the grouping of Eurostat crops and the public catalogue of harmonised layers that some inputs come from. The INCA plugin
[@inca2026] informed the sequence of preprocessing steps and the form of the activity index. The calculations in this report
are carried out by esa-toolbox.
:::

# Limitations

**Potential.** Potential is an indicator of environmental suitability and does not count pollinators or visits to flowers. The
model does not include pesticides or fertilisers, for which data are lacking across time and space, and it covers wild solitary
bees and bumblebees only. The land cover scores are expert judgements, and the method does not attach uncertainty to them. Using
the separate edge scores of Table S3 in @zulian2013 would raise the suitability of forest edges by 0.1, an effect that we have
not measured. The service providing area is a threshold, so a small change in potential can move a cell in or out of it. The
road map is one snapshot, so it does not contribute to change over time.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="method-original"}
The bumblebee layer is static, so it does not contribute to change over time either, and the change in potential leans on the
climate of the expert-based model.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-meta="method-original"}
**Bumblebees.** The species models are those fitted to the records and layers of 2012, and a projection assumes that each species
keeps the same relation to its environment. The layers of each year are rebuilt from current releases of their sources, and the
accounts use the projection for change only, so the level of the bumblebee layer remains that of the published layer of 2012. One
presence threshold serves all species in place of the thresholds of the fitted models. The climate layers describe 22 years, so
the bumblebee layer responds to climate gradually, and it does not show the effect of a single hot or dry year. Every layer is
limited to the range of the fitted models, so a climate warmer than any of 2012 counts as the warmest then observed.
:::

**Crops.** Demand and yield come from a model that disaggregates regional data to 1 km, so the location of a crop within a region
is an estimate. The crop area and yield of 2018 stand in for 2024, which is the largest assumption in the series. Demand is
reported in the hectares of CAPRI, which for flax and hemp are several times those of Eurostat, although this crop group weighs
little in the flow.[\ Dependency ratios are fixed literature values, and more recent reviews propose different values for some
crops.]{.content-visible when-meta="method-original"}[\ Dependency ratios are means of field experiments from many regions and cultivars, and the ratio of a
crop group is the simple mean of its crops, so it does not reflect which crops and cultivars of the group are grown in each
country.]{.content-visible unless-meta="method-original"}

**Flow.** Actual flow treats a crop as pollinated when it grows in the service providing area, with no measure of how much
pollination it receives. Changes in flow also reflect changes in production for reasons other than pollination, so change in the
area of met demand is the better guide to change in the service. Values for Croatia, Malta and Cyprus, and for the few other crops
without a place on the map, are estimates that assume the crop is spread across the agricultural land of the country. Cyprus and
Malta could enter the crop maps in future, since the later CAPRI series holds area for them.

**Value.** The valuation attributes to pollination a share of the value of production at basic price, without removing the costs
of farmers, so it measures a contribution to value and does not measure a rent. A consumer price index converts the values to 2010
prices, so the constant series removes general inflation and leaves changes in relative crop prices in place. Value per tonne is
uniform within a crop and country, so maps of value inherit the physical pattern. Other valuation methods exist
[@vallecillo2018], and they would give different figures.

**Maps at 100 m.** These maps keep the total of each kilometre, and they are not meant to be read cell by cell. Where the crop
data place crops in a kilometre in which Corine shows few agricultural cells, those cells receive the whole value, so a single 1
hectare cell can show more area or tonnes than a hectare could hold. Sums over areas of a kilometre or more are the reliable
reading.
